tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

55	**exploring**
56	: Mode of work for a question that the record does not settle. You gather evidence, first in the record and then in the original tree. You add what you found to the record, and then go back to building.
57	
58	You work with three things: your brief, the record and the original tree. Building happens in one area at a time, so this skill has one part for each area.
59	
60	## How a program runs
61	
62	Walk and the compiled path share the parser and the phases below. After those, they share almost no code, so a fix on one path does not reach the other. If you edit a phase that both paths run, or a class under `nativeHelpers/` that a `builtinPrimitive` string of the interpreter's library names (`references/interpreter.md`, "Natives"), run your test on both paths. `references/compiler.md`, "Natives", says how to test such a class on the compiled path. If you record a defect that the record does not hold, and its program can run on the other path, run it there too. Say in the ledger row which paths show the defect. The Java and Scala paths in this skill are under `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/`.
63	
64	### The phases
65	
66	Each path runs these phases on each component, in this order (`compiler/phases/PhaseOrder.java`):
67	
68	1. Parse the source into a syntax tree. This tree is the only form of the program, from the parser to the bytecode.
69	2. Bind each name to its declaration.
70	3. Expand the DSL grammars that the component imports (`references/build-and-caches.md`).
71	4. Check the static types. Walk's phase list holds this phase, but walk switches it off.
72	5. Desugar: comprehensions and big operators become calls, and getters and setters become methods.
73	6. Mark each call of an overloaded name.
74	
75	Walk then interprets the tree. The tree has no static types, so walk finds a type error only at run time, as a failed dispatch. A program that runs under walk can be ill-typed, unlike in Java or Scala.
76	
77	`fortress compile` runs the same phases with the static type checker, in Scala, switched on. Before the checker, it folds integer literals. After the phases, the code generator writes JVM bytecode into a jar. A type error stops the compile.
78	
79	Each path has its own library today. At the switch-over, the compiled path moves onto the interpreter's library, and the compiler's prelude, three files of its library, is deleted (`references/compiler.md`). The compiled checker already finds no error in the interpreter's library. For the `FortressLibrary` component, the count stage shows this as a total of 0 (`references/compiler.md`). The switch-over waits for walk's natives: each function that the interpreter's library binds with `builtinPrimitive` (`references/interpreter.md`, "Natives") must first have a binding that the compiled path runs.
80	
81	### The compiled runtime
82	
83	`fortress run` compiles no Fortress source. It runs the jars of the program and of the library on the JVM. A jar holds JVM class files:
84	
85	- the component's functions, objects and traits;
86	- its closures;
87	- one dispatch method for each overloaded name. It tests the run-time types of all the arguments, from the most specific declaration to the least specific. Walk also chooses at run time.
88	
89	A generic declaration is compiled once, as a template class. The first time that a program uses an instantiation, such as `Box[\RR64\]`, the class loader makes its class. It copies the template's bytecode, puts in the static arguments, and loads the result. A static argument is a type, or a size as a descriptor from `RTTIsize.of`. These classes are never on disk. C# specialises generics in this way. Java erases them.
90	
91	The class loader is code of this tree that the revival changes, so a failure while a class loads can be its defect (`references/compiler.md`).
92	
93	HotSpot, the JVM's compiler, then compiles the hot bytecode to machine code. A number is a boxed object, also inside a specialised class: `RR64` is the class `FRR64`. An array is a library object, read and written through its `get` and `put` methods.
94	
95	### The caches
96	
97	A run keeps the results of its phases in the caches, so that a later run can reuse them. The caches are folders in `default_repository/caches/`, or in a private caches folder that a run names. An entry is one file in a cache, written for one source file.
98	
99	- `interpreter_parsed_cache/`: walk's parsed tree of each file, `X-<hash>.tfi` for an api and `X-<hash>.tfs` for a component.
100	- `interpreter_cache/`: walk's tree of each component after the phases. Walk loads it back and interprets it. The entry is a text dump of the tree. It starts `(Component @"/home/user/fortress/Library/FlatString.fss" ...`.
101	- `analyzed_cache/`: the results of the phases that `fortress compile` reuses.
102	- `bytecode_cache/`: one jar for each compiled component.
103	
104	In the first three caches, `<hash>` is a hash of the source's absolute path, and the entry holds that path. So the entries of a tree copied to another path must be renamed and rewritten. `explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh` does this (`references/worktrees.md`).
105	
106	`references/build-and-caches.md` says when a run reuses an entry, and when the build empties the caches.
107	
108	### Parallelism and mutable state
109	
110	Fortress evaluates in parallel by default, not in Java's left-to-right order. The iterations of a `for` loop, the elements of a tuple, and the arguments and operands of a call can run at once. A loop is sequential only if every generator is `seq(...)`. The parallel parts run as tasks on a work-stealing pool, the fork/join pool of Doug Lea (a `java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool`). `FORTRESS_THREADS` sets its number of threads. Tasks, transactions and the pool are built twice, independently: for walk in `interpreter/evaluator/tasks/`, and for the compiled path in `runtimeSystem/`.
111	
112	`x = e` declares an immutable variable. `var x: T = e` and `x: T := e` declare a mutable one, and `x := e` assigns to it (`Specification/basic/variables.tex`). These are Scala's `val` and `var`, or Swift's `let` and `var`. A field is immutable unless it is declared with `var`. A value object is a tuple, `()`, or an object whose declaration, or a trait that it extends, has the `value` modifier, as the library's numbers, characters and booleans do. It has only immutable fields and value semantics, like a Swift `struct`. Any other object, except a function, is a reference object, like an instance of a Swift class. Each construction makes a new reference object, distinct from all others (`Specification/basic/objects.tex:24-33`).
113	
114	Parallel code stays free of races in these ways:
115	
116	- Most data is immutable.
117	- A big operator, such as `SUM` or `BIG MAX`, combines the results of its tasks, as OpenMP's reduction clause does. No task writes a shared accumulator. The specification's reduction variables are not built.
118	- A write to shared state goes inside an `atomic` block. This is software transactional memory, like Haskell's `atomically` (`Specification/basic/evaluation/parallelism.tex`). The programmer writes `atomic`; the compiler adds none.
119	- Tasks can write different elements of one array in parallel (`Specification/basic/memory-model.tex`, "Programming Discipline").
120	
121	So `acc := acc + x` inside a parallel `for`, with no `atomic`, is a race. The suites run at four threads, once each, so a race can show in them. A passing run does not prove that there is none.
122	
123	Inside an `atomic` block, the compiled code tracks each mutable variable that the block reads or writes. From the switch-over, it also tracks each array element that the block reads or writes (`references/compiler.md`).
124	
125	## Fortress as a language
126	
127	Each point below corrects an assumption from a language that you know. `references/tests-writing.md` gives the form of a program.
128	
129	- **Dispatch is on every argument, at run time.** A call chooses among overloads by the run-time types of all its arguments, as in Julia, not by static types as in Java. The checker accepts two overloads only if their parameter types exclude each other, one is strictly more specific, or a third covers their meet. The more specific one's return type must fit the other's. Walk checks part of this at load.
130	- **Functional methods.** A method with `self` among its parameters is called `f(x)`, not `x.f()`. It overloads with top-level functions. Most operators are declared so: `opr +(self, other: T): T`. A functional method's name is reserved in every program that imports it, so do not name a variable after it. One type must not have a dotted and a functional method of the same name.
131	- **Traits and objects, no classes.** A trait has methods and abstract fields, and extends several traits. An object is a leaf. `excludes {A, B}` says that no value has both types. `comprises {A, B}` says that every value has a listed type, near Scala's `sealed`. No type may extend two instantiations of one generic trait. This exclusion rule is why the number types are flat (below).
132	- **Static parameters.** They are written `[\T\]`, and `[i]` indexes. Their kinds are types, sizes (`nat` is an `NN32` value, `int` a `ZZ32`), `bool` and `opr`. Generics are invariant: there is no `+T` or `-T`. An unbounded type parameter is bounded by `Any`, which holds tuples, functions and `()`, as `Object` does not. A type parameter that a call does not fix takes its bound. Under walk, one whose bound names the parameter itself stays open, and every value passes it. Walk instantiates a reduction or a comprehension without static arguments at the type declared for its value: a local variable's type, or a top-level or local function's return type. Without one, it uses the join, the least common supertype, of its elements' run-time types. Some other cases still get the empty type `Bottom` under walk (`references/revival-changes.md`, "Static parameters").
133	- **Numbers are siblings, not a tower.** `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `ZZ`, `QQ`, `RR32` and `RR64` are siblings under `Number`. None is a subtype of another, unlike Haskell's classes or Java's widening. A wider type declares a `coerce` from each narrower one. A conversion never changes which declaration runs when one already fits. Overflow raises `IntegerOverflow`. The algebra is self-typed traits, such as `AdditiveGroup[\T\]` with `+`, not monoids over an operator parameter. `references/library.md` gives the rest: ranges, wrapping, `SUM`.
134	- **Loops and reductions are library code.** `for`, comprehensions and `SUM` call the library's generators and reductions (`references/library.md`).
135	- **Juxtaposition is an operator, and whitespace counts.** `f x` applies a function. Otherwise juxtaposition is an operator that the library overloads: `2 x` multiplies, and `"a" "b"` concatenates. How three juxtaposed items group depends on their types, unlike in Haskell. An infix operator has whitespace on both sides or on neither: `a -b` is a static error. Precedence is partial: `a + b ∪ c` needs parentheses.
136	- **Specified, but not built:** dimensions and units, `property` declarations, regions and complex numbers. Some constructs run only under walk (`references/compiler.md`).
137	
138	## The record

The switch-over waits for walk's natives: each function that the interpreter's library binds with `builtinPrimitive` (`references/interpreter.md`, "Natives") must first have a binding that the compiled path runs.

### The compiled runtime

`fortress run` compiles no Fortress source. It runs the jars of the program and of the library on the JVM. A jar holds JVM class files:

- the component's functions, objects and traits;
- its closures;
- one dispatch method for each overloaded name. It tests the run-time types of all the arguments, from the most specific declaration to the least specific. Walk also chooses at run time.

A generic declaration is compiled once, as a template class. The first time that a program uses an instantiation, such as `Box[\RR64\]`, the class loader makes its class. It copies the template's bytecode, puts in the static arguments, and loads the result. A static argument is a type, or a size as a descriptor from `RTTIsize.of`. These classes are never on disk. C# specialises generics in this way. Java erases them.

The class loader is code of this tree that the revival changes, so a failure while a class loads can be its defect (`references/compiler.md`).

HotSpot, the JVM's compiler, then compiles the hot bytecode to machine code. A number is a boxed object, also inside a specialised class: `RR64` is the class `FRR64`. An array is a library object, read and written through its `get` and `put` methods.

### The caches

A run keeps the results of its phases in the caches, so that a later run can reuse them. The caches are folders in `default_repository/caches/`, or in a private caches folder that a run names. An entry is one file in a cache, written for one source file.

- `interpreter_parsed_cache/`: walk's parsed tree of each file, `X-<hash>.tfi` for an api and `X-<hash>.tfs` for a component.
- `interpreter_cache/`: walk's tree of each component after the phases. Walk loads it back and interprets it. The entry is a text dump of the tree. It starts `(Component @"/home/user/fortress/Library/FlatString.fss" ...`.
- `analyzed_cache/`: the results of the phases that `fortress compile` reuses.
- `bytecode_cache/`: one jar for each compiled component.

In the first three caches, `<hash>` is a hash of the source's absolute path, and the entry holds that path. So the entries of a tree copied to another path must be renamed and rewritten. `explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh` does this (`references/worktrees.md`).

`references/build-and-caches.md` says when a run reuses an entry, and when the build empties the caches.

### Parallelism and mutable state

Fortress evaluates in parallel by default, not in Java's left-to-right order. The iterations of a `for` loop, the elements of a tuple, and the arguments and operands of a call can run at once. A loop is sequential only if every generator is `seq(...)`. The parallel parts run as tasks on a work-stealing pool, the fork/join pool of Doug Lea (a `java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool`). `FORTRESS_THREADS` sets its number of threads. Tasks, transactions and the pool are built twice, independently: for walk in `interpreter/evaluator/tasks/`, and for the compiled path in `runtimeSystem/`.

`x = e` declares an immutable variable. `var x: T = e` and `x: T := e` declare a mutable one, and `x := e` assigns to it (`Specification/basic/variables.tex`). These are Scala's `val` and `var`, or Swift's `let` and `var`. A field is immutable unless it is declared with `var`. A value object is a tuple, `()`, or an object whose declaration, or a trait that it extends, has the `value` modifier, as the library's numbers, characters and booleans do. It has only immutable fields and value semantics, like a Swift `struct`. Any other object, except a function, is a reference object, like an instance of a Swift class. Each construction makes a new reference object, distinct from all others (`Specification/basic/objects.tex:24-33`).

Parallel code stays free of races in these ways:

- Most data is immutable.
- A big operator, such as `SUM` or `BIG MAX`, combines the results of its tasks, as OpenMP's reduction clause does. No task writes a shared accumulator. The specification's reduction variables are not built.
- A write to shared state goes inside an `atomic` block. This is software transactional memory, like Haskell's `atomically` (`Specification/basic/evaluation/parallelism.tex`). The programmer writes `atomic`; the compiler adds none.
- Tasks can write different elements of one array in parallel (`Specification/basic/memory-model.tex`, "Programming Discipline").

So `acc := acc + x` inside a parallel `for`, with no `atomic`, is a race. The suites run at four threads, once each, so a race can show in them. A passing run does not prove that there is none.

Inside an `atomic` block, the compiled code tracks each mutable variable that the block reads or writes. From the switch-over, it also tracks each array element that the block reads or writes (`references/compiler.md`).

## Fortress as a language

Each point below corrects an assumption from a language that you know. `references/tests-writing.md` gives the form of a program.

- **Dispatch is on every argument, at run time.** A call chooses among overloads by the run-time types of all its arguments, as in Julia, not by static types as in Java. The checker accepts two overloads only if their parameter types exclude each other, one is strictly more specific, or a third covers their meet. The more specific one's return type must fit the other's. Walk checks part of this at load.
- **Functional methods.** A method with `self` among its parameters is called `f(x)`, not `x.f()`. It overloads with top-level functions. Most operators are declared so: `opr +(self, other: T): T`. A functional method's name is reserved in every program that imports it, so do not name a variable after it. One type must not have a dotted and a functional method of the same name.
- **Traits and objects, no classes.** A trait has methods and abstract fields, and extends several traits. An object is a leaf. `excludes {A, B}` says that no value has both types. `comprises {A, B}` says that every value has a listed type, near Scala's `sealed`. No type may extend two instantiations of one generic trait. This exclusion rule is why the number types are flat (below).
- **Static parameters.** They are written `[\T\]`, and `[i]` indexes. Their kinds are types, sizes (`nat` is an `NN32` value, `int` a `ZZ32`), `bool` and `opr`. Generics are invariant: there is no `+T` or `-T`. An unbounded type parameter is bounded by `Any`, which holds tuples, functions and `()`, as `Object` does not. A type parameter that a call does not fix takes its bound. Under walk, one whose bound names the parameter itself stays open, and every value passes it. Walk instantiates a reduction or a comprehension without static arguments at the type declared for its value: a local variable's type, or a top-level or local function's return type. Without one, it uses the join, the least common supertype, of its elements' run-time types. Some other cases still get the empty type `Bottom` under walk (`references/revival-changes.md`, "Static parameters").
- **Numbers are siblings, not a tower.** `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `ZZ`, `QQ`, `RR32` and `RR64` are siblings under `Number`. None is a subtype of another, unlike Haskell's classes or Java's widening. A wider type declares a `coerce` from each narrower one. A conversion never changes which declaration runs when one already fits. Overflow raises `IntegerOverflow`. The algebra is self-typed traits, such as `AdditiveGroup[\T\]` with `+`, not monoids over an operator parameter. `references/library.md` gives the rest: ranges, wrapping, `SUM`.
- **Loops and reductions are library code.** `for`, comprehensions and `SUM` call the library's generators and reductions (`references/library.md`).
- **Juxtaposition is an operator, and whitespace counts.** `f x` applies a function. Otherwise juxtaposition is an operator that the library overloads: `2 x` multiplies, and `"a" "b"` concatenates. How three juxtaposed items group depends on their types, unlike in Haskell. An infix operator has whitespace on both sides or on neither: `a -b` is a static error. Precedence is partial: `a + b ∪ c` needs parentheses.
- **Specified, but not built:** dimensions and units, `property` declarations, regions and complex numbers. Some constructs run only under walk (`references/compiler.md`).

A `run` fails if the program exits non-zero or a `run_*` check fails. With no `run_out` check, its output must contain `pass` or `PASS`. For example:

    tests=EqualityRung1
    link
    run
    run_out_WIcontains=PASS

## How `XXX` works

- Under walk, an `XXX` test is `tests/XXXName.fss`, whose component is `XXXName`. With no `.test` file, it is green when it fails as a plain test would.
- In the compiled test folders, the `XXX` prefix of a `.test` file's name applies to every command that the file drives: each must fail. So a defect at run time, whose link succeeds, needs two `.test` files ("Writing an `XXX` test").
- An unmet `run_*` check makes a run test red, whatever the prefix.
- The harness reports any link or compile exception of a component whose name contains `XXX` as expected, whatever the `.test` file's name. Only an unmet key of that command makes it red.
- An `XXX` compile test with a `compile_err_contains` key, whose program compiles, reports "Saw wrong failure", which is red.
- A green `XXX` test prints `Saw expected failure` or `OK Saw expected exception`.

## How a defect is recorded

Record every defect that you measure in one of three ways, and say in your report which:

1. Your change repairs it: an assertion in your plain gated test. It needs no `XXX` stage.
2. It is deferred, and the specification settles it: a gated `XXX` test that asserts the specification's answer. Write it in the change that measured the defect, even if a later change will repair it. If walk crashes on the program, still write the `XXX` test, unlike under 3: the harness counts the crash as the expected failure. A deferred defect of a program that the checker accepts and that then fails the JVM's verification (`VerifyError`), linkage or a range check at run time is one of these.
3. It is deferred, and the specification is silent or a conflict leaves it open (`exploring.md`): a test that asserts today's behaviour, and a row in the gap ledger (`records.md`). If no program can observe the defect, or no gated test can pass while it shows, as when walk crashes on the program, write the ledger row only. Its reproducer, the row's cell that names the test, is `none`, and its notes give the command and its output.

If your brief does not let you edit the original tree, say in your report which of the three the defect needs, and write a ledger row for it, whichever it needs. A probe that only measures and reports is an example. The change that next works there writes the test.

1. Write the test, with a plain name. Write the essence of the defect as a clean, minimal program, not the shape in which a probe met it.
2. See the test fail through the harness (`harness-one.sh` or `junit.sh`, `tests-running.md`) on the base's code. Do this in a run that ends before you first build or compile your edit. Under walk, do it before you edit a library source that the test reads. If your tree already holds the fix, run the test through the harness on the old code, as `worktrees.md`, "Running the old code", says.
3. Make the fix. See the test pass in your last run after your last change of code.

The test needs no commit of its own. A test that comes with no fix, such as one that guards a behaviour that works today, has no failing run: see it pass through the harness.

Assert a value with `assert` in an interpreter test. In a compiled test, assert it with `assert` (above), or print it and check it with a `run_out_equals` key. The harness checks both, so they are part of the suite's verdict.

An edit of prose in `Specification/` or `Documentation/` has no test. Check it as `specification.md`, "Changing the text: the revision form", says.

1	# The compiled checker, the code generator and the runtime
2	
3	**count stage**
4	: Script that runs the compiled checker over the interpreter's library, on the `FortressLibrary` component and the apis that it imports, and prints the errors in a table: `explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh`. Its total is the checker count.
5	
6	**distance stage**
7	: Stage of the gate that runs the compiled checker over fourteen components of the interpreter's library, `FortressLibrary` among them, runs each of the checker's steps on each component whatever the earlier steps report, and prints the errors in a table. Your brief gives its command when you need it.
8	
9	The code of this area is in these directories:
10	
11	- `scala_src/typechecker/`: the type checker, in Scala.
12	- `compiler/`: the disambiguator, the desugarers, overloading, `codegen/`, `NamingCzar` and `OverloadSet`.
13	- `runtimeSystem/`: `InstantiatingClassloader`, tasks and transactions.
14	
15	The phases' names in the code are parse, PREDISAMBIGUATEDESUGAR, DISAMBIGUATE, GRAMMAR, PRETYPECHECKDESUGAR, INTEGERLITERALFOLDING, TYPECHECK, DESUGAR, OVERLOADREWRITE and CODEGEN.
16	
17	## What the two paths share
18	
19	After the phases, each path has its own code for these:
20	
21	- Values: walk's `interpreter/evaluator/values/` (`FInt`, `FFloat`), and the compiled `compiler/runtimeValues/` (`FZZ32`, `FRR64`).
22	- Number natives: walk's glue classes, in `interpreter/glue/prim/` (`Int.java`, `Long.java`).
23	- Dispatch: walk searches at run time, in `OverloadedFunction`. The compiled path calls a dispatch method that `OverloadSet` generates.
24	- The run: `fortress run` starts a second JVM (`bin/run`), which never enters `Shell.java`.
25	
26	Both paths run the helpers, the public static methods of classes under `nativeHelpers/`.
27	
28	The phases differ too: walk turns off some desugarings that the compiled path runs (`interpreter.md`, "Where a fix of walk belongs"). A fix of one of those desugarers changes only the compiled path.
29	
30	## The compiler's prelude, until the switch-over
31	
32	The compiled path uses the compiler's own prelude: `LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss`, `Library/CompilerLibrary.fss` and `Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss`. `Library/CompilerSystem.fss` is the compiled path's `System`.
33	
34	Do not add a declaration to the three prelude files: they are deleted at the switch-over. Their tests stay. If a helper of `nativeHelpers/` that the one library binds is wrong, fix the helper's Java, even where the prelude binds it too. Do not edit the prelude's text: its binding then gives the fixed result. If a compiled test pinned the old result, change the test with the helper, as for any fixed defect.
35	
36	## What the compiled path cannot compile yet
37	
38	For a construct that it cannot compile yet, the code generator calls `sayWhat` or throws another `CompilerError`. Such a call or throw is a code-generator wall. The code generator has no case for these constructs:
39	
40	- `label` and `exit`, `spawn`, and `atomic` used as an expression;
41	- an object expression;
42	- an array literal, such as `[1 2 3]`.
43	
44	It compiles a local function as a closure, also one that calls itself or another local function of its block. It refuses these forms (ledger row 304):
45	
46	- a local function with static parameters of its own: 'Can't compile a local function with static parameters of its own yet';
47	- two local functions of one name in a block: 'Can't compile overloaded local functions yet';
48	- a local function with the `atomic` modifier: 'Can't compile a local function with this modifier yet'.
49	
50	A type assumption `e asif T` has the value of `e`, but the call around it chooses its declaration as if `e` were a `T`, a supertype of `e`'s type (`Specification/basic/expressions/type-annotation.tex`). The code generator compiles one at a dotted call's receiver, at a call of a functional method or an overloaded function whose every argument is an assumption, and elsewhere as the value of `e`. It refuses these forms (ledger row 818):
51	
52	- a call of a functional method or an overloaded function with an assumption at some of its arguments but not all: 'Can't compile a dispatched call whose arguments are not all type assumptions';
53	- a generic method on an assumed receiver: 'Can't compile a type assumption at the receiver of a generic method yet';
54	- a call of an overloaded generic function with an assumption at an argument: 'Can't compile a type assumption at a call of an overloaded generic function yet'.
55	
56	It also refuses a function or method with a contract (`requires`, `ensures`, `invariant`). It compiles a declaration whose own header or `extends` entry has a `where` clause, and emits nothing for the clause. A call of a function or method whose own clause introduces a `where`-clause variable, as `where [\nat n\]` does, links, but dies at run time with `NoClassDefFoundError` (ledger row 867). `compiler_tests/XXXWhereVariableCallCompiled.test` records it: copy its form for such a call. The disambiguator, which both paths run, drops a trait's or object's contract, so the code generator never sees one, and walk does not check one either (ledger row 781). It refuses a function or method with a modifier other than `getter`, `setter`, `io`, `private`, `abstract` and `test`, such as `override` (ledger row 650). A trait or object that extends a generic trait compiles with `Any` as the static argument. With `Bottom`, `Self` or an abbreviated type there, the code generator refuses the declaration. An abbreviated type is a short form, such as `RR64[3]` for an array type. With a tuple that holds `Any` there, the code generator crashes (ledger row 889).
57	
58	The compiler's prelude has no array types, only `ZZ32Vector` and `StringVector`. Its `for` loops, comprehensions and reductions work over `ZZ32` ranges only. Its reductions give a `ZZ32` or a `String`.
59	
60	Until the switch-over, a compiled test uses none of these. If a test needs one, write it as an `XXX` test that names the wall (`tests-writing.md`).
61	
62	## What the code generator does
63	
64	- It emits no primitive `double` arithmetic.
65	- The class loader rewrites a template's bytes with ASM. The emitted classfiles stay at version 1.6, because this rewriting keeps no stack-map frames. Do not raise the version.
66	- The `value` modifier adds the mark interface `ValueObjectMark` to the object's class. The compiled `SEQV` (`nativeHelpers/equality.java`) reads the mark. The modifier does not inline or unbox the fields.
67	- An array of `RR64` values is to be stored as an unboxed `double[]`. The code generator does not build it yet. If your task touches how arrays are stored, print the two POSITIONS entries on arrays first (about 2 KB):
68	
69	      explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'positions:array is stored as' 'positions:array design'
70	
71	## The runtime
72	
73	- The class loader is `runtimeSystem/InstantiatingClassloader.java`. The revival has changed it for sizes and for the lock on a class's first load (ledger row 417). Before you investigate a failure while a class loads, read ledger rows 408 and 559, which name it (`records.md`, "Reading the record").
74	- The compiled code keeps each mutable variable in a cell (`compiler/runtimeValues/MutableFValue.java`). Before each read and write of the cell, the generated code asks `BaseTask.inATransaction()` (`runtimeSystem/`). Inside an `atomic` block, the access goes through the transaction. So the transaction tracks the variables that the block touches. From the switch-over, it also tracks each element of the one library's arrays, by array and index: `compiler/runtimeValues/FortressArrayStore.java` calls the transaction's methods `TXReadSlot` and `TXWriteSlot`. Walk does not run this class, so test an edit of it with `ArrayStoreJUTest`, beside it.
75	
76	## Natives
77	
78	`import java com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.{...}` in a `.fss` file binds static Java methods over plain Java values.
79	
80	A body `builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.Class.method")` binds one such method, a helper, too. In a compile, at the parse, the compiled path, and not walk, rewrites the body as a call of the method through a generated `import java`, with `self` first in a trait or object (`compiler/BuiltinPrimitiveRewriter.java`). The checker then checks the declaration against the method's Java signature. In a compile, it reads `int` as `ZZ32`, `long` as `ZZ64`, `float` as `RR32`, `double` as `RR64`, `boolean` as `Boolean`, `String` as `JavaString`, `BigInteger` as `ZZ` and `Object` as `Any` (`NamingCzar.fortressTypeForForeignJavaType`). The compile stops in these cases:
81	
82	- If the string is in that package but names no public static method: 'builtinPrimitive names no static helper: …'.
83	- If the string names a glue class or anything else outside that package: 'Variable builtinPrimitive is not defined.'
84	- If the declaration has a varargs parameter: the same message (ledger row 849).
85	- If the declaration is a local function or a method of an object expression: the same message. The rewrite reaches only a component's declarations and the members of its traits and objects (ledger row 865).
86	
87	The rewrite runs only in a JVM that has made a Fortress repository of the compiled path, the compiler's store of components, not this git repository. Walk's repository switches it off again. `fortress compile` makes one, and so do `disambiguate`, `grammar`, `desugar` and `typecheck` (`Shell.compilerPhases`). `fortress parse` and `fortress api` make none, so they rewrite a body only after a compile in the same JVM (ledger row 882). Alone, they pass a misspelt helper. Test a binding with `compile`. In a suite, the result of `parse` or `api` depends on whether a compile ran earlier in the same JVM.
88	
89	To test a helper on the compiled path, write a compiled test whose own declarations bind it, as `compiler_tests/NativeHelperBindingCompiled.fss` does. Until the switch-over, a compiled test cannot reach the interpreter's library's bindings.
90	
91	The count stage and the distance stage check the interpreter's library with the same rewrite. There, the checker differs from a compile in these ways:
92	
93	- A string that names a glue class, or a declaration with a varargs parameter, does not stop the check. The body stays a call of `builtinPrimitive`, typed at the declared result type, and no Java signature checks it (ledger row 849).
94	- The checker reads a helper's Java types as the interpreter's library's types: `String` as `String`, not `JavaString`, and the rest as in a compile.
95	- A component that imports a DSL grammar is parsed by other code (`GraphRepository.syntaxExpand`), which does not rewrite its bindings. So, as for a glue class, no Java signature checks them.
96	- The count stage checks only the `FortressLibrary` component's bindings. A binding of another component, as `FortressBuiltin`'s, only the distance stage checks.
97	
98	The checker, in a compile and in both stages, reads `int` as `NN32` or `Char`, and `long` as `NN64`, only for six transfer helpers with fixed names (`NamingCzar.java:373-384`, `:494-503`). Where a binding gives a parameter, `self` or the result the type `NN32`, `NN64` or `Char`, or a parameter or `self` the type `UnsignedLong` (the one library's object that extends `NN64`), and the helper has `int` or `long` there, the rewrite passes that value through the matching transfer helper. A result declared `UnsignedLong` gets none. `self` gets a transfer helper only in a method of one of these four types itself. The transfer helpers return their argument unchanged. So the checker accepts such a binding whatever helper it names, a signed one included, as `simpleIntArith.intLT` for `NN32`'s `<`. If you move a binding over these types onto a helper, test it on both paths at values where a signed and an unsigned reading differ (2^31 and above for `NN32`, 2^63 and above for `NN64`), as `compiler_tests/NativeHelperFamilyNN32Compiled.fss` and `tests/NativeHelperFamilyNN32Walk.fss` do. If the class has more than one method of the helper's name and number of parameters, the rewrite adds no transfer helper. The checker then reports 'Could not check call to function builtinPrimitive_<Class>_<method>', followed by '… is not applicable to an argument of type …'.
99	
100	The wrapper generator wraps every method of a class that it is given, the private methods too. If a type has no Fortress counterpart, it fails the whole import. So give every method of a helper class a signature that maps to Fortress, also a private method. In the count stage and the distance stage, a type maps only if the interpreter's library declares it. So there, a binding stops its component if any method of its helper's class has a type that only the compiler's prelude declares. The distance stage then counts the component as a stopped target. `nativeHelpers/systemOps` is such a class: its `getArgs` answers `StringVector`, so the message is 'FortressBuiltin.StringVector is undefined.' (F-321). Bind a helper of another class.
101	
102	## Traps of the compiled path
103	
104	- The compiler's prelude declares `print`, `println` and `String`'s `||` at `Object`, not `Any` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi:37`, `:55`, `:61`). So until the switch-over, the checker refuses a generic that prints a value of a type parameter written without a bound, or concatenates it onto a `String`. The message names `Object`, as 'Object->() is not applicable to an argument of type T.' does for `println`. In such a generic of a compiled program or test, write `T extends Object`. The generic then takes no tuple, function or `()`. The one library declares these operations at `Any` or `String`, so do not change its text for this limit.
105	- A `try`'s `forbid` clause lists exception types: an exception of a listed type that no `catch` clause took is wrapped in a `ForbiddenException`, which the `try` throws. A `try`'s `finally` clause does not run when an exception leaves the `try` block: one that no `catch` clause takes, or that `ForbiddenException` (ledger row 890). So write no compiled program that relies on `finally` after an exception leaves the `try`. A test that needs it is an `XXX` test (`tests-writing.md`). In a `try` nested in another `try` of one body, the outer `try`'s `catch` clause is matched first (ledger row 888). A `try` whose block can throw, with a `finally` clause and no `catch` or `forbid` clause, fails with a `VerifyError` at class load (ledger row 891).
106	- Each evaluation of a string literal makes a new string object, so `"ab" SEQV "ab"` is `false` (ledger row 945). A test of it asserts `true`, as an `XXX` test.
107	- An api and the component that implements it must have the same name. If there is none, the link fails ("Could not find an implementation for API"), and the run dies with `NoClassDefFoundError`.
108	- The compiled dispatch ignores the contravariance of a parameter of arrow type. The property `fortress.disable.contravariance` is true by default, so `OverloadSet` passes no variance. If a compiled call with function arguments picks another declaration than walk does, look here first.
109	- A clean link does not prove that every call has its method. Two calls die at run time with `NoSuchMethodError`:
110	  - a call of a functional method of an object that a trait's `comprises` clause lists, on a value whose static type is the object. An example is `num(R)`, where `trait Q comprises { R }` declares `abstract num(self): ZZ32` and `object R extends Q` gives its body. Call it through a value typed as the trait, as `q: Q = R` and then `num(q)` (ledger row 815);
111	  - a read of an exported object's value parameter, from a component that imports the api, where the exporting component names the parameter otherwise than the api. A value parameter is a parameter of the object's constructor, and also a field. An example is `Np(3).a`, where the api declares `object Np(a: ZZ32)` and the component `object Np(z: ZZ32)`. The export check compares no value parameter's name. Give each value parameter the api's name (ledger row 839).
112	
113	## The checker's gaps
114	
115	- Overloads: in its test of whether two domains exclude each other, the checker puts the meet of a static parameter's declared bounds in the parameter's place where the parameter is a whole parameter type, an element of a tuple or a member of an intersection or union (P-157). Inside a static argument, as `T` in `Box[\T\]`, the parameter stays. The paths differ on `tint[\T extends Red\](x: Box[\T\])` beside `tint[\T extends Blue\](x: Box[\T\])`, where `Red`, `Blue` and `Box` are objects. The checker refuses it, because `Box[\Bottom\]` lies in both domains, and walk loads it. No decision says which is right. Assert neither path's answer in a test (ledger row 786).
116	- A `where` clause's constraint: the checker checks a function's or functional method's constraint on its own static parameters at the call. At a dotted call, a candidate is not applicable where the receiver's static argument breaks the method's constraint. A trait's or object's own constraint is checked where its type is used, also at a constructor call; only the checker reads it, and the compiled code does not check it. A `where`-clause variable is a static parameter of the function's arrow type, inferred at the call. The checker does not yet check these, and no ledger row holds the first two:
117	  - at a dotted call, a constraint whose bound names the method's own static parameters or a `where`-clause variable;
118	  - at a type's use, a constraint whose bound names a `where`-clause variable;
119	  - a static argument written at a top-level call, against its parameter's bound (ledger row 470).
120	- Imports: `import A.{...}`, with the three dots written, imports every name of `A`. The overloading check also reads `A`'s declarations of a name that the component imports by name from another api. So `import A.{...}` beside `import B.{ pick }`, where both apis declare `pick(x: P)`, is refused: 'There are multiple declarations of pick' (ledger row 813). Leave the name out of the whole import, as `import A.{...} except { pick }`.
121	- An `except` clause leaves out each identifier that it lists, on both paths. Neither path leaves out an infix operator that it lists. So where a component lists `-` in `except` and declares its own `-` at the api's parameter types, the code generator stops. Walk runs the component's own `-` (ledger row 814).
122	- Conditional extension: the condition holds while the checker checks the `extends` entry itself, an object's value parameters and every member. It does not hold for the other `extends` entries, the static parameters, the declaration's own `where` clause, and the `excludes` and `comprises` clauses. The checker lets a member that it checked under the condition be called where the condition fails (ledger row 773).
123	- A `comprises` clause that lists a type at a `where`-clause variable, as `NatParam comprises { N[\n\] } where [\ nat n \]` or `AnyList comprises List[\E\] where [\E\]`: at a call, the checker gives the variable a fresh size or type, equal only to itself. Two values passed in one call get two. A fresh type is bounded by the binding and by the clause's constraints. The variable is in scope in the trait, except in its `extends` and `excludes` clauses. The checker gives no fresh type where it meets the trait as a supertype of another type. Where a generic type that the clause lists, as `List[\E\]`, gives the body of a member of the trait, the code generator crashes: 'E is not in the kind env' (ledger row 812). Where the variable is a size, a compiled call that passes a value of such a trait where a listed type is expected fails the JVM's verification (ledger row 307). Departures: a fresh type also under a function type's result (ledger row 751), none for an extender that the clause does not list (ledger row 752), and a crash at a call, from outside the trait, of a member whose type names the variable (ledger row 756).
124	
125	## The `fortress` commands
126	
127	`Shell.java` dispatches `bin/fortress <command>`.
128	
129	- To see what an early phase makes of a program, stop after that phase: `parse` (a syntax check), `disambiguate`, `grammar`, `desugar` or `typecheck`.
130	- `unparse` prints the syntax tree back as Fortress source. Use it to see what a desugaring made.
131	- `link` links a compiled component (the `link` step of a compiled `.test` file). `api` writes a component's api. `test` runs a program's `test` declarations under walk.
132	- The command chooses the library. Walk and `test` call `Shell.useInterpreterLibraries()`. Every other command calls `useCompilerLibraries()`. Each call points `WellKnownNames` and `Types` to its prelude, and sets the desugaring switches.
133	
134	## Running
135	
136	    cd ProjectFortress
137	    # after an ant compileAll that started the caches again: the library order (build-and-caches.md)
138	    ../bin/fortress compile <path>/P.fss
139	    ../bin/fortress run P [args]
140	
141	A small program compiles in about 5 s and runs in about 1 s.
142	
143	- A crash of the checker prints one line and hides the Java stack. To see the stack, put `-debug stacktrace` before the file: `../bin/fortress compile -debug stacktrace <path>/P.fss`.
144	- A failed compile of a program leaves a 0-byte jar in `bytecode_cache/`. A run of the program then prints "Could not load P" and "Resource not found". Read the compile's error instead.
145	
146	## Before an edit
147	
148	Two notes under `explorations/coordinator/map/` help you find where a fix belongs. A status or a line number in them can be stale. Before you rely on a status, read the ledger rows that it cites. Before you rely on a line number, grep for the method's name.
149	
150	- Before you add or fix a language feature, print its row of the feature table. WORD names the feature, such as `spawn`, `coercion` or `typecase`. A row is about 1 KB. It names the feature's section of the specification, its parser rule, checker class, walk site, code-generator site, prelude declaration and ledger rows.
151	
152	      explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'map:spec-to-implementation.md#Feature by feature@WORD'
153	
154	- If your edit is in one phase, and you need what runs before and after it on each path, print that phase's section. Name the section by its number and the first word of its title. A section is 1 to 3 KB. B.1 is the phase list, B.4 disambiguation, B.5 desugaring, B.6 type checking, B.7 overloading, B.10 the caches, B.11 the runtime and B.12 the natives.
155	
156	      explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'map:modules-and-phases.md#B.5 Desugaring'
157	
158	- Before you change the text of a diagnostic, grep the `.test` files for it. A `.test` file can pin a whole diagnostic with `compile_err_equals`, its `file:line:column` included. `grep -l 'TEXT' ProjectFortress/*tests/*.test`, with words of the diagnostic as TEXT, lists the files that pin it. Update each of those in the same commit. A line that you add to or remove from a compiler test program moves the pinned spans below it.
159	
160	## Testing an edit here
161	
162	- For a quick loop on an edit of the checker or the code generator, compile the edited class into a scratch directory, and run the compiler with that directory first on its class path. Give each run a fresh copy of the caches, because nothing checks the caches against the compiler that wrote them, and a compile of an unchanged program with a jar writes nothing:
163	
164	      Q=$PWD/tmp/quick ; export FORTRESS_CACHES=$Q/caches ; CP=$(bin/fortress_classpath | tail -1)
165	      mkdir -p $Q/classes && javac -nowarn -cp "$CP" -d $Q/classes ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/<path>/X.java
166	      rm -rf $Q/caches && cp -a default_repository/caches $Q/caches
167	      java $JAVA_FLAGS -Dfile.encoding=UTF-8 -Dfortress.caches=$Q/caches -cp "$Q/classes:$CP" com.sun.fortress.Shell compile P.fss
168	      bin/fortress run P
169	
170	  For a Scala file, compile it with `java -cp "$CP" scala.tools.nsc.Main -classpath "$CP" -d $Q/classes -encoding UTF-8 X.scala`. Then put the edit into the tree and build it for real.
171	- If your change is near transactions, top-level mutable state or the class loader's first load, do the four-thread atomic runs (`gate.md`).
172	
173	## The checker's time
174	
175	This section is for a change of the checker: its Scala under `scala_src/`, or `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast` and the generators under `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/astgen/`, from which the build generates the checker's syntax tree and `Walker`.
176	
177	The count stage takes `<out-file> <scratch>` and about 80 to 180 seconds, more under load. It can run past the Bash tool's 120-second limit, so run it in the background (`session.md`). It writes a table to the out-file: the errors of each api, the total, the number of places with errors, and the first crash. It keeps the checker's whole output in `<scratch>/run.txt`, and its caches in `<scratch>`, so a run from the base build leaves the base build as it was.
178	
179	The checker checks every api first, and the component only if no api has an error. In each api or component, it stops at the first of its stages that finds errors. The stages run in this order (`compiler/StaticChecker.java`, `checkCompilationUnit`):
180	
181	1. The type hierarchy and the type check.
182	2. The overloading check, which also compares the overloads' return types.
183	3. In the component only, the export check (`library.md`, "Designing a change").
184	
185	So the count misses the errors of the later stages, and a fix of an early error can raise it.
186	
187	The table's rows tell a clean run from a run that the checker did not finish:
188	
189	- `#total 0` and `#locations 0`: the checker reached the component and found no error.
190	- `#stopped`, in place of `#total` and `#locations`: the errors came from a phase before the checker, such as the parse. The checker reported none and did not reach the component. The script exits 1, and the gate reads the table as red.
191	- `#crash`: the first crash of the overloading check that the run survived, or `none`.
192	
193	If the run printed no error total and was not clean, the script writes no table and exits 1.
194	
195	The checker's results are the programs that it accepts and refuses, and each error with its text and its place. On the interpreter's library, a change keeps the results the same if both of these hold:
196	
197	- The two tables are equal: `diff` prints nothing.
198	- The two `run.txt` files are equal after you replace each run's own tree path with one word, such as `TREE`. Any difference fails.
199	
200	A node's hash starts from its class name, so an order in the output, such as the apis' checks, does not vary from run to run. A moved order is a difference: keep the old order, or report it.
201	
202	`Walker`, in the generated `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/nodes/FortressAst.scala`, is split into methods under 8,000 bytes of bytecode. HotSpot does not compile a longer method, and the walker runs on every node. `MethodSizeJUTest` fails if a method of the build grows past the limit, except the methods that its source lists in `listed(...)` entries. Run it alone with `ant testOnly -DtestPattern=MethodSizeJUTest`. If a method of `Walker` fails, lower `WALKER_CASES_PER_METHOD` in `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/astgen/ScalaAstGenerator.java`. If another method fails, split it under the limit. List it only if nothing in the checker or a compiled run calls it, with its size and what runs it, and name it in your report.
203	
204	The timing is a smoke test, to catch a slowdown of several times. One run of each tree is enough. A small difference, or one within the noise from run to run, is not a finding. In your report, say what you saw, and do not analyse it.
205	
206	If you change the checker:
207	
208	1. Make the change correct, with its tests. Commit it, and name the commit in your report.
209	2. Time the base build and the change, named `base` and `change`. Run the base in a call set up for the base build (`build-and-caches.md`), and the change in a call set up for your tree, each in the background (`session.md`). Use the same command for both, with `N` the run's name:
210	
211	       export W=<your tree> N=base ; mkdir -p $W/tmp/count
212	       time explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh $W/tmp/count/$N.txt $W/tmp/count/$N
213	
214	3. Make a second pass that makes the checker faster. Start with a profile (below). Where the profile shows a gain, take it. Where it shows none, say so in your report, with the profile's top frames.
215	4. If the second pass changed code, run the count stage once more with the command of step 2, named `pass`. Show that its results are the same as `change`'s. Then run `ant testQuick` once more (`tests-running.md`, "When to run a whole suite"). If it changed nothing, run neither, and report `change`'s results in place of `pass`'s.
216	5. If the pass reuses an answer that the checker computed earlier, as a memo does, audit it on one full run. Put the audit in an instrumented copy ("Testing an edit here"), never in the tree. In the audit, compute each reused answer again and compare the two. If any answer differs, the reuse is wrong: fix it or drop it, then repeat step 4. Report the count of reuses and of differences.
217	6. In your report, give each run's seconds, the diff of the `base` and `change` tables, the comparison of their `run.txt` files, and that `pass` has the same results as `change`.
218	
219	To find where the time goes, use JFR on the count stage's checker, instrumented copies compiled into a scratch folder ahead of the build on the class path, and the methods over 8,000 bytes that `MethodSizeJUTest` lists in its source. A profiled or instrumented run is neither a timed run nor a run to compare. Print the commands of two earlier speed probes (about 8 KB):
220	
221	    explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/perf-probes/checker-speed-2/REPORT.md#Decisions, findings' 'doc:explorations/perf-probes/checker-speed/REPORT.md#Decisions, findings'
222	
223	If your brief asks you to review a change of the checker, run the count stage yourself. Time the base build and the worker's commit of step 1 once each, as step 2 says, with the commit and the worker's head in worktrees seeded at them (`worktrees.md`). Check that your times are the worker's, in order of size. Check that the commit's and the head's results are the same.

# The compiled checker, the code generator and the runtime

**count stage**
: Script that runs the compiled checker over the interpreter's library, on the `FortressLibrary` component and the apis that it imports, and prints the errors in a table: `explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh`. Its total is the checker count.

**distance stage**
: Stage of the gate that runs the compiled checker over fourteen components of the interpreter's library, `FortressLibrary` among them, runs each of the checker's steps on each component whatever the earlier steps report, and prints the errors in a table. Your brief gives its command when you need it.

The code of this area is in these directories:

- `scala_src/typechecker/`: the type checker, in Scala.
- `compiler/`: the disambiguator, the desugarers, overloading, `codegen/`, `NamingCzar` and `OverloadSet`.
- `runtimeSystem/`: `InstantiatingClassloader`, tasks and transactions.

The phases' names in the code are parse, PREDISAMBIGUATEDESUGAR, DISAMBIGUATE, GRAMMAR, PRETYPECHECKDESUGAR, INTEGERLITERALFOLDING, TYPECHECK, DESUGAR, OVERLOADREWRITE and CODEGEN.

## What the two paths share

After the phases, each path has its own code for these:

- Values: walk's `interpreter/evaluator/values/` (`FInt`, `FFloat`), and the compiled `compiler/runtimeValues/` (`FZZ32`, `FRR64`).
- Number natives: walk's glue classes, in `interpreter/glue/prim/` (`Int.java`, `Long.java`).
- Dispatch: walk searches at run time, in `OverloadedFunction`. The compiled path calls a dispatch method that `OverloadSet` generates.
- The run: `fortress run` starts a second JVM (`bin/run`), which never enters `Shell.java`.

Both paths run the helpers, the public static methods of classes under `nativeHelpers/`.

The phases differ too: walk turns off some desugarings that the compiled path runs (`interpreter.md`, "Where a fix of walk belongs"). A fix of one of those desugarers changes only the compiled path.

## The compiler's prelude, until the switch-over

The compiled path uses the compiler's own prelude: `LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss`, `Library/CompilerLibrary.fss` and `Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss`. `Library/CompilerSystem.fss` is the compiled path's `System`.

Do not add a declaration to the three prelude files: they are deleted at the switch-over. Their tests stay. If a helper of `nativeHelpers/` that the one library binds is wrong, fix the helper's Java, even where the prelude binds it too. Do not edit the prelude's text: its binding then gives the fixed result. If a compiled test pinned the old result, change the test with the helper, as for any fixed defect.

## What the compiled path cannot compile yet

For a construct that it cannot compile yet, the code generator calls `sayWhat` or throws another `CompilerError`. Such a call or throw is a code-generator wall. The code generator has no case for these constructs:

- `label` and `exit`, `spawn`, and `atomic` used as an expression;
- an object expression;
- an array literal, such as `[1 2 3]`.

It compiles a local function as a closure, also one that calls itself or another local function of its block. It refuses these forms (ledger row 304):

- a local function with static parameters of its own: 'Can't compile a local function with static parameters of its own yet';
- two local functions of one name in a block: 'Can't compile overloaded local functions yet';
- a local function with the `atomic` modifier: 'Can't compile a local function with this modifier yet'.

A type assumption `e asif T` has the value of `e`, but the call around it chooses its declaration as if `e` were a `T`, a supertype of `e`'s type (`Specification/basic/expressions/type-annotation.tex`). The code generator compiles one at a dotted call's receiver, at a call of a functional method or an overloaded function whose every argument is an assumption, and elsewhere as the value of `e`. It refuses these forms (ledger row 818):

- a call of a functional method or an overloaded function with an assumption at some of its arguments but not all: 'Can't compile a dispatched call whose arguments are not all type assumptions';
- a generic method on an assumed receiver: 'Can't compile a type assumption at the receiver of a generic method yet';
- a call of an overloaded generic function with an assumption at an argument: 'Can't compile a type assumption at a call of an overloaded generic function yet'.

It also refuses a function or method with a contract (`requires`, `ensures`, `invariant`). It compiles a declaration whose own header or `extends` entry has a `where` clause, and emits nothing for the clause. A call of a function or method whose own clause introduces a `where`-clause variable, as `where [\nat n\]` does, links, but dies at run time with `NoClassDefFoundError` (ledger row 867). `compiler_tests/XXXWhereVariableCallCompiled.test` records it: copy its form for such a call. The disambiguator, which both paths run, drops a trait's or object's contract, so the code generator never sees one, and walk does not check one either (ledger row 781). It refuses a function or method with a modifier other than `getter`, `setter`, `io`, `private`, `abstract` and `test`, such as `override` (ledger row 650). A trait or object that extends a generic trait compiles with `Any` as the static argument. With `Bottom`, `Self` or an abbreviated type there, the code generator refuses the declaration. An abbreviated type is a short form, such as `RR64[3]` for an array type. With a tuple that holds `Any` there, the code generator crashes (ledger row 889).

The compiler's prelude has no array types, only `ZZ32Vector` and `StringVector`. Its `for` loops, comprehensions and reductions work over `ZZ32` ranges only. Its reductions give a `ZZ32` or a `String`.

Until the switch-over, a compiled test uses none of these. If a test needs one, write it as an `XXX` test that names the wall (`tests-writing.md`).

## What the code generator does

- It emits no primitive `double` arithmetic.
- The class loader rewrites a template's bytes with ASM. The emitted classfiles stay at version 1.6, because this rewriting keeps no stack-map frames. Do not raise the version.
- The `value` modifier adds the mark interface `ValueObjectMark` to the object's class. The compiled `SEQV` (`nativeHelpers/equality.java`) reads the mark. The modifier does not inline or unbox the fields.
- An array of `RR64` values is to be stored as an unboxed `double[]`. The code generator does not build it yet. If your task touches how arrays are stored, print the two POSITIONS entries on arrays first (about 2 KB):

      explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'positions:array is stored as' 'positions:array design'

## The runtime

- The class loader is `runtimeSystem/InstantiatingClassloader.java`. The revival has changed it for sizes and for the lock on a class's first load (ledger row 417). Before you investigate a failure while a class loads, read ledger rows 408 and 559, which name it (`records.md`, "Reading the record").
- The compiled code keeps each mutable variable in a cell (`compiler/runtimeValues/MutableFValue.java`). Before each read and write of the cell, the generated code asks `BaseTask.inATransaction()` (`runtimeSystem/`). Inside an `atomic` block, the access goes through the transaction. So the transaction tracks the variables that the block touches. From the switch-over, it also tracks each element of the one library's arrays, by array and index: `compiler/runtimeValues/FortressArrayStore.java` calls the transaction's methods `TXReadSlot` and `TXWriteSlot`. Walk does not run this class, so test an edit of it with `ArrayStoreJUTest`, beside it.

## Natives

`import java com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.{...}` in a `.fss` file binds static Java methods over plain Java values.

A body `builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.Class.method")` binds one such method, a helper, too. In a compile, at the parse, the compiled path, and not walk, rewrites the body as a call of the method through a generated `import java`, with `self` first in a trait or object (`compiler/BuiltinPrimitiveRewriter.java`). The checker then checks the declaration against the method's Java signature. In a compile, it reads `int` as `ZZ32`, `long` as `ZZ64`, `float` as `RR32`, `double` as `RR64`, `boolean` as `Boolean`, `String` as `JavaString`, `BigInteger` as `ZZ` and `Object` as `Any` (`NamingCzar.fortressTypeForForeignJavaType`). The compile stops in these cases:

- If the string is in that package but names no public static method: 'builtinPrimitive names no static helper: …'.
- If the string names a glue class or anything else outside that package: 'Variable builtinPrimitive is not defined.'
- If the declaration has a varargs parameter: the same message (ledger row 849).
- If the declaration is a local function or a method of an object expression: the same message. The rewrite reaches only a component's declarations and the members of its traits and objects (ledger row 865).

The rewrite runs only in a JVM that has made a Fortress repository of the compiled path, the compiler's store of components, not this git repository. Walk's repository switches it off again. `fortress compile` makes one, and so do `disambiguate`, `grammar`, `desugar` and `typecheck` (`Shell.compilerPhases`). `fortress parse` and `fortress api` make none, so they rewrite a body only after a compile in the same JVM (ledger row 882). Alone, they pass a misspelt helper. Test a binding with `compile`. In a suite, the result of `parse` or `api` depends on whether a compile ran earlier in the same JVM.

To test a helper on the compiled path, write a compiled test whose own declarations bind it, as `compiler_tests/NativeHelperBindingCompiled.fss` does. Until the switch-over, a compiled test cannot reach the interpreter's library's bindings.

The count stage and the distance stage check the interpreter's library with the same rewrite. There, the checker differs from a compile in these ways:

- A string that names a glue class, or a declaration with a varargs parameter, does not stop the check. The body stays a call of `builtinPrimitive`, typed at the declared result type, and no Java signature checks it (ledger row 849).
- The checker reads a helper's Java types as the interpreter's library's types: `String` as `String`, not `JavaString`, and the rest as in a compile.
- A component that imports a DSL grammar is parsed by other code (`GraphRepository.syntaxExpand`), which does not rewrite its bindings. So, as for a glue class, no Java signature checks them.
- The count stage checks only the `FortressLibrary` component's bindings. A binding of another component, as `FortressBuiltin`'s, only the distance stage checks.

The checker, in a compile and in both stages, reads `int` as `NN32` or `Char`, and `long` as `NN64`, only for six transfer helpers with fixed names (`NamingCzar.java:373-384`, `:494-503`). Where a binding gives a parameter, `self` or the result the type `NN32`, `NN64` or `Char`, or a parameter or `self` the type `UnsignedLong` (the one library's object that extends `NN64`), and the helper has `int` or `long` there, the rewrite passes that value through the matching transfer helper. A result declared `UnsignedLong` gets none. `self` gets a transfer helper only in a method of one of these four types itself. The transfer helpers return their argument unchanged. So the checker accepts such a binding whatever helper it names, a signed one included, as `simpleIntArith.intLT` for `NN32`'s `<`. If you move a binding over these types onto a helper, test it on both paths at values where a signed and an unsigned reading differ (2^31 and above for `NN32`, 2^63 and above for `NN64`), as `compiler_tests/NativeHelperFamilyNN32Compiled.fss` and `tests/NativeHelperFamilyNN32Walk.fss` do. If the class has more than one method of the helper's name and number of parameters, the rewrite adds no transfer helper. The checker then reports 'Could not check call to function builtinPrimitive_<Class>_<method>', followed by '… is not applicable to an argument of type …'.

The wrapper generator wraps every method of a class that it is given, the private methods too. If a type has no Fortress counterpart, it fails the whole import. So give every method of a helper class a signature that maps to Fortress, also a private method. In the count stage and the distance stage, a type maps only if the interpreter's library declares it. So there, a binding stops its component if any method of its helper's class has a type that only the compiler's prelude declares. The distance stage then counts the component as a stopped target. `nativeHelpers/systemOps` is such a class: its `getArgs` answers `StringVector`, so the message is 'FortressBuiltin.StringVector is undefined.' (F-321). Bind a helper of another class.

## Traps of the compiled path

- The compiler's prelude declares `print`, `println` and `String`'s `||` at `Object`, not `Any` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi:37`, `:55`, `:61`). So until the switch-over, the checker refuses a generic that prints a value of a type parameter written without a bound, or concatenates it onto a `String`. The message names `Object`, as 'Object->() is not applicable to an argument of type T.' does for `println`. In such a generic of a compiled program or test, write `T extends Object`. The generic then takes no tuple, function or `()`. The one library declares these operations at `Any` or `String`, so do not change its text for this limit.
- A `try`'s `forbid` clause lists exception types: an exception of a listed type that no `catch` clause took is wrapped in a `ForbiddenException`, which the `try` throws. A `try`'s `finally` clause does not run when an exception leaves the `try` block: one that no `catch` clause takes, or that `ForbiddenException` (ledger row 890). So write no compiled program that relies on `finally` after an exception leaves the `try`. A test that needs it is an `XXX` test (`tests-writing.md`). In a `try` nested in another `try` of one body, the outer `try`'s `catch` clause is matched first (ledger row 888). A `try` whose block can throw, with a `finally` clause and no `catch` or `forbid` clause, fails with a `VerifyError` at class load (ledger row 891).
- Each evaluation of a string literal makes a new string object, so `"ab" SEQV "ab"` is `false` (ledger row 945). A test of it asserts `true`, as an `XXX` test.
- An api and the component that implements it must have the same name. If there is none, the link fails ("Could not find an implementation for API"), and the run dies with `NoClassDefFoundError`.
- The compiled dispatch ignores the contravariance of a parameter of arrow type. The property `fortress.disable.contravariance` is true by default, so `OverloadSet` passes no variance. If a compiled call with function arguments picks another declaration than walk does, look here first.
- A clean link does not prove that every call has its method. Two calls die at run time with `NoSuchMethodError`:
  - a call of a functional method of an object that a trait's `comprises` clause lists, on a value whose static type is the object. An example is `num(R)`, where `trait Q comprises { R }` declares `abstract num(self): ZZ32` and `object R extends Q` gives its body. Call it through a value typed as the trait, as `q: Q = R` and then `num(q)` (ledger row 815);
  - a read of an exported object's value parameter, from a component that imports the api, where the exporting component names the parameter otherwise than the api. A value parameter is a parameter of the object's constructor, and also a field. An example is `Np(3).a`, where the api declares `object Np(a: ZZ32)` and the component `object Np(z: ZZ32)`. The export check compares no value parameter's name. Give each value parameter the api's name (ledger row 839).

## The checker's gaps

- Overloads: in its test of whether two domains exclude each other, the checker puts the meet of a static parameter's declared bounds in the parameter's place where the parameter is a whole parameter type, an element of a tuple or a member of an intersection or union (P-157). Inside a static argument, as `T` in `Box[\T\]`, the parameter stays. The paths differ on `tint[\T extends Red\](x: Box[\T\])` beside `tint[\T extends Blue\](x: Box[\T\])`, where `Red`, `Blue` and `Box` are objects. The checker refuses it, because `Box[\Bottom\]` lies in both domains, and walk loads it. No decision says which is right. Assert neither path's answer in a test (ledger row 786).
- A `where` clause's constraint: the checker checks a function's or functional method's constraint on its own static parameters at the call. At a dotted call, a candidate is not applicable where the receiver's static argument breaks the method's constraint. A trait's or object's own constraint is checked where its type is used, also at a constructor call; only the checker reads it, and the compiled code does not check it. A `where`-clause variable is a static parameter of the function's arrow type, inferred at the call. The checker does not yet check these, and no ledger row holds the first two:
  - at a dotted call, a constraint whose bound names the method's own static parameters or a `where`-clause variable;
  - at a type's use, a constraint whose bound names a `where`-clause variable;
  - a static argument written at a top-level call, against its parameter's bound (ledger row 470).
- Imports: `import A.{...}`, with the three dots written, imports every name of `A`. The overloading check also reads `A`'s declarations of a name that the component imports by name from another api. So `import A.{...}` beside `import B.{ pick }`, where both apis declare `pick(x: P)`, is refused: 'There are multiple declarations of pick' (ledger row 813). Leave the name out of the whole import, as `import A.{...} except { pick }`.
- An `except` clause leaves out each identifier that it lists, on both paths. Neither path leaves out an infix operator that it lists. So where a component lists `-` in `except` and declares its own `-` at the api's parameter types, the code generator stops. Walk runs the component's own `-` (ledger row 814).
- Conditional extension: the condition holds while the checker checks the `extends` entry itself, an object's value parameters and every member. It does not hold for the other `extends` entries, the static parameters, the declaration's own `where` clause, and the `excludes` and `comprises` clauses. The checker lets a member that it checked under the condition be called where the condition fails (ledger row 773).
- A `comprises` clause that lists a type at a `where`-clause variable, as `NatParam comprises { N[\n\] } where [\ nat n \]` or `AnyList comprises List[\E\] where [\E\]`: at a call, the checker gives the variable a fresh size or type, equal only to itself. Two values passed in one call get two. A fresh type is bounded by the binding and by the clause's constraints. The variable is in scope in the trait, except in its `extends` and `excludes` clauses. The checker gives no fresh type where it meets the trait as a supertype of another type. Where a generic type that the clause lists, as `List[\E\]`, gives the body of a member of the trait, the code generator crashes: 'E is not in the kind env' (ledger row 812). Where the variable is a size, a compiled call that passes a value of such a trait where a listed type is expected fails the JVM's verification (ledger row 307). Departures: a fresh type also under a function type's result (ledger row 751), none for an extender that the clause does not list (ledger row 752), and a crash at a call, from outside the trait, of a member whose type names the variable (ledger row 756).

## The `fortress` commands

`Shell.java` dispatches `bin/fortress <command>`.

- To see what an early phase makes of a program, stop after that phase: `parse` (a syntax check), `disambiguate`, `grammar`, `desugar` or `typecheck`.
- `unparse` prints the syntax tree back as Fortress source. Use it to see what a desugaring made.
- `link` links a compiled component (the `link` step of a compiled `.test` file). `api` writes a component's api. `test` runs a program's `test` declarations under walk.
- The command chooses the library. Walk and `test` call `Shell.useInterpreterLibraries()`. Every other command calls `useCompilerLibraries()`. Each call points `WellKnownNames` and `Types` to its prelude, and sets the desugaring switches.

## Running

    cd ProjectFortress
    # after an ant compileAll that started the caches again: the library order (build-and-caches.md)
    ../bin/fortress compile <path>/P.fss
    ../bin/fortress run P [args]

A small program compiles in about 5 s and runs in about 1 s.

- A crash of the checker prints one line and hides the Java stack. To see the stack, put `-debug stacktrace` before the file: `../bin/fortress compile -debug stacktrace <path>/P.fss`.
- A failed compile of a program leaves a 0-byte jar in `bytecode_cache/`. A run of the program then prints "Could not load P" and "Resource not found". Read the compile's error instead.
